# What Snakemake is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

Snakemake runs workflows written as rules, in a file named `Snakefile`, in
Python extended with a syntax for rules. A rule says how to make files of one
pattern from files of another, such as `results/fits/{station}.parquet` from
`results/clean/{station}.parquet`. Like Make, Snakemake starts from the files it
is asked for and works backward: it finds the rule whose output matches each
name, then the files that rule needs, and so on, back to files that exist. It
then runs the jobs whose outputs are missing or out of date, in order, and at
the same time where it can. Almost everything that surprises newcomers follows
from that: rules that never run, names that match the wrong rule, and jobs that
run again, or do not (@sec-model). Working with Snakemake comes down to writing
rules, asking what would run, and running them on a laptop or a cluster
(@sec-usage).

[](index.qmd) explains what Snakemake shares with Nextflow and states the rules
for both.

Checked against Snakemake 9.27.0.


# How Snakemake thinks {#sec-model}

Snakemake makes files. Every run starts from the files asked for, follows the
rules backward to the files that exist, and then forward again, running each
job whose outputs are missing or out of date.


## Rules, wildcards, and jobs {#sec-rules}

```python
rule fit:
    input:
        "results/clean/{station}.parquet",
    output:
        "results/fits/{station}.parquet",
    shell:
        "stationfit fit {input} --output {output}"
```

A rule has inputs, outputs, and a way to make the one from the other: a shell
command, a script, or Python code. `{station}` is a wildcard, which makes the
output not a file but a pattern, matching every name of that form. A job is a
rule with its wildcards filled in: asked for `results/fits/007.parquet`,
Snakemake sets `station` to `007`, and the job needs
`results/clean/007.parquet`. Wildcards take their values from the output only,
so every wildcard of the inputs must appear in it. In the command, `{input}`
and `{output}` stand for the files of the job.


## Nothing runs that no target asks for {#sec-targets}

Snakemake makes its targets: the files named on the command line, or, without
any, the inputs of the first rule of the Snakefile, by convention a rule `all`
that only lists the final results. It does not look at what the directories
hold, only at what the targets need. A rule that no target needs, directly or
through other rules, never runs, and a new station in `data/raw/` is not
processed until a target names a result of it. The list of the stations
therefore belongs in the configuration, from which `expand` makes the list of
targets (@sec-snakefile); `glob_wildcards` reads it from the names of existing
files instead, where a directory is the list.

The same model makes it cheap to ask for less: `snakemake
results/fits/007.parquet` runs only what this one file needs.


## A wildcard matches anything {#sec-patterns}

A wildcard matches any text of at least one character, slashes and dots
included. The output `results/{station}.parquet` also matches
`results/fits/007.parquet`, with `station` set to `fits/007`. Snakemake decides
which rule makes a file by which rule's inputs it can find or make, and stops
with an `AmbiguousRuleException` where it could use both, so the outcome
depends on which files happen to exist. Give the outputs of each rule a
directory of their own, such as `results/clean/` and `results/fits/`, and
constrain the wildcards whose values have a form, such as with
`wildcard_constraints` and `station=r"\d{3}"` (@sec-snakefile). A file name is
the interface between two rules, like the signature of a function.

The values of a wildcard are text, and so are the codes of stations in the
configuration only when quoted. YAML reads `[007, 012]` as the numbers 7 and
10, the second in octal, and Snakemake then looks for `data/raw/7.csv` and
`data/raw/10.csv`; write `["007", "012"]`.


## Out of date: what makes a job run again {#sec-triggers}

A job runs if one of its outputs is missing, or if Snakemake finds a reason in
what it recorded when it last made them, in `.snakemake/metadata/`:

| Trigger | The job runs again when |
|----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `mtime` | An input is newer than the outputs; for an input of up to 1 MB, only if its checksum has changed too |
| `input` | The set of its input files has changed |
| `params` | A value of its `params` has changed |
| `code` | Its command or its script has changed, even if only by a comment |
| `software-env` | Its Conda environment or its container has changed |

Every job that reads what a job made again runs as well, down to the targets.
`snakemake --dry-run` lists each job that would run, with its reason
(@sec-dry-run).

Snakemake sees only what the rule declares. A value of the configuration that a
script reads itself, such as `snakemake.config["threshold"]`, is no parameter of
the rule: changing it runs nothing again, and the old results stay
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-declared-inputs)). Pass every value that a
step uses through `params`. A module that the script imports, or a package
updated in an environment that is not pinned, is no part of the rule's code
either.

The times of the files mislead in both directions. A large input copied without
its times, such as onto a new disk, makes everything after it run again,
although nothing changed; `ancient()` around an input tells Snakemake to ignore
its time. `snakemake --touch` marks every output as up to date without running
anything, even outputs whose parameters have changed. That is right after
moving a finished workflow and wrong after any change: it hides exactly the
stale outputs that the triggers are there to find.


## A failed job leaves nothing behind {#sec-incomplete}

Snakemake runs shell commands with Bash in strict mode, `set -euo pipefail`, so
a command whose pipe fails halfway fails
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-all-or-nothing)). When a job fails,
Snakemake deletes its outputs, which may be incomplete, and keeps its log, to
find out why.

When Snakemake itself is killed, such as by the time limit of the job it runs
in, the outputs of the jobs that were running stay, marked as incomplete, and
the next run refuses to start until told what to do with them:
`--rerun-incomplete` makes them again. A killed run also leaves the directory
locked; `snakemake --unlock` releases it, once no other run is using it.


# Working with Snakemake {#sec-usage}

The examples are a workflow that cleans the measurements of each station, fits
a model to each, and summarizes the fits. A package does the science, with a
command for each step, `stationfit clean` and `stationfit fit`, and a function
for the summary ([](index.qmd#sec-thin)).


## Lay out a workflow {#sec-layout}

```default
workflow/
    Snakefile           the rules
    envs/               one Conda environment per step
    scripts/            the scripts that rules run with script:
config/
    config.yaml         the stations and the parameters
profiles/
    slurm/config.yaml   the settings for the cluster
    test/config.yaml    the settings for the test
.tests/                 a small dataset, with a config/ of its own
results/                what the workflow makes
logs/                   what its jobs report
```

Snakemake runs in the directory it is started from, the top of this layout, and
finds `workflow/Snakefile` by itself. The paths of inputs, outputs, logs, and
the configuration are relative to that directory, and those of `script:` and
`conda:` relative to the Snakefile. A large workflow splits its rules into files
of their own, such as `workflow/rules/fit.smk`, which the Snakefile includes
with `include: "rules/fit.smk"`.


## Write the rules {#sec-snakefile}

```python
# workflow/Snakefile
configfile: "config/config.yaml"


wildcard_constraints:
    station=r"\d{3}",


rule all:
    input:
        "results/summary.parquet",


rule clean:
    input:
        "data/raw/{station}.csv",
    output:
        "results/clean/{station}.parquet",
    conda:
        "envs/stationfit.yaml"
    shell:
        "stationfit clean {input} --output {output}"


rule fit:
    input:
        "results/clean/{station}.parquet",
    output:
        "results/fits/{station}.parquet",
    params:
        seed=config["seed"],
    threads: 4
    resources:
        mem_mb=8000,
        runtime=60,
    log:
        "logs/fit/{station}.log",
    conda:
        "envs/stationfit.yaml"
    shell:
        "stationfit fit {input} --output {output} "
        "--seed {params.seed} --threads {threads} 2> {log}"


rule summarize:
    input:
        expand("results/fits/{station}.parquet", station=config["stations"]),
    output:
        "results/summary.parquet",
    conda:
        "envs/stationfit.yaml"
    script:
        "scripts/summarize.py"
```

```yaml
# config/config.yaml
stations: ["007", "012", "031"]
seed: 42
```

`expand` fills the pattern with every station of the configuration, and so
makes the inputs of `summarize`, the one job that needs all fits. `params`
carries the seed into the command and into the records of the job, so that a
new seed runs the fits again (@sec-triggers). `threads` is the number of CPUs
of a job, which `{threads}` passes to the program, and `resources` its memory,
in megabytes, and its time, in minutes, which a cluster grants it (@sec-run).
`log` names a file for the messages of the job, which the command writes into
itself, here with `2> {log}`.

```python
# workflow/scripts/summarize.py
from stationfit import summarize

summarize(list(snakemake.input), output=snakemake.output[0])
```

A script named by `script:` receives an object `snakemake` with the inputs,
outputs, parameters, threads, and wildcards of its job, such as
`snakemake.input` and `snakemake.params.seed`; in R, `snakemake@input` and
`snakemake@params[["seed"]]`. Such a script runs only under Snakemake, so keep
it to a few lines that call the package, which can be tested without it.


## Ask what would run {#sec-dry-run}

```bash
snakemake --dry-run                           # the jobs that would run, and why
snakemake --dry-run results/fits/007.parquet  # only what this file needs
snakemake --summary                           # every output, with its state
snakemake --dag | dot -Tsvg > dag.svg         # the graph, as a figure
snakemake --forcerun fit                      # run fit again, and what follows
```

A dry run takes a second and shows what Snakemake makes of the targets, the
rules, and the files on disk, with the reason for each job (@sec-triggers). Run
one before every real run; a job that should not run, or a hundred jobs where
three were expected, shows up there rather than in the results. `--summary`
lists every output with its date, its rule, and whether it would be made again.


## Run on a laptop and on a cluster {#sec-run}

```bash
snakemake --cores 8 --sdm conda      # on this machine
snakemake --profile profiles/slurm   # on the cluster
snakemake --profile profiles/test    # the test, on any machine
```

On a single machine, `--cores` is required, and it caps the CPUs of all jobs
that run at once. `--sdm conda` creates the environment of each rule from its
file, once, in `.snakemake/conda/`, and runs the jobs of the rule in it;
`--sdm apptainer` does the same with the images of `container:`, and
`--apptainer-args` passes options to Apptainer, such as those of
[](../containers/apptainer.qmd#sec-host). An environment file may name only
packages, without versions; a pin file beside it, such as
`envs/stationfit.linux-64.pin.txt`, which `snakedeploy pin-conda-envs` writes,
fixes every version ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)).

```yaml
# profiles/slurm/config.yaml
executor: slurm
jobs: 100
software-deployment-method: conda
default-resources:
  slurm_partition: cpu
  slurm_account: ocean-lab
  mem_mb: 2000
  runtime: 30
```

A profile is a directory with a file `config.yaml`, whose keys are the options
of the command line without their dashes ([](index.qmd#sec-profiles)). On a
cluster, the executor `slurm`, from the package
`snakemake-executor-plugin-slurm`, submits every job as a Slurm job, with the
`threads` and `resources` of its rule, and `jobs` limits how many wait or run
at once. `default-resources` holds for every rule that does not set its own.
Snakemake itself runs on the login node, where the cluster allows it, in a
session that survives logging out ([](index.qmd#sec-executor)).

```yaml
# profiles/test/config.yaml
directory: .tests
cores: 2
software-deployment-method: conda
```

The test runs the same workflow in `.tests/`, which holds a small dataset in
`data/raw/` and a configuration of its own in `config/config.yaml`, so that its
results never mix with the real ones
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-end-to-end)). After a run that counts,
`snakemake --report report.html`, with the same options, writes a report of the
jobs, their code, parameters, environments, and run times
([](index.qmd#sec-records)); it needs the Python package pygments.
